An upper bound for the type of a numerical semigroup,
and a reduction of Wilf’s conjecture

Mohammad F. Marashdeh Address: Department of Mathematics, Mutah University, Karak, Jordan Email address: marashdeh@mutah.edu.jo
Abstract.

Let SS be a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m\mathrm{m}, conductor c\mathrm{c}, embedding dimension e\mathrm{e}, type t\mathrm{t} and genus g\mathrm{g}, and let n=c−g\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{g}. Wilf’s conjecture asserts that e​n≥c\mathrm{e}\,\mathrm{n}\geq\mathrm{c}; the inequality g≤t​n\mathrm{g}\leq\mathrm{t}\,\mathrm{n} of Fröberg, Gottlieb and Häggkvist settles it when t≤e−1\mathrm{t}\leq\mathrm{e}-1. The Apéry set of SS with respect to any s∈S∖{0}s\in S\setminus\{0\} carries a partial order whose maximal elements are the pseudo-Frobenius numbers translated by ss; for s=ms=\mathrm{m} its minimal elements are the minimal generators other than m\mathrm{m}. Comparing the two extremal statistics bounds the type by t≤e−1+Ξ⁡(S)≤e−1+Θ⁡(S)\mathrm{t}\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\Xi(S)\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\Theta(S), where Θ⁡(S)\Theta(S) measures the redundancy of the covering of the gaps of SS by the pseudo-Frobenius numbers and Ξ⁡(S)\Xi(S) refines it. With an exact decomposition of the Wilf number this yields the genus bound g≤e−1+t⁡(n−1)\mathrm{g}\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\mathrm{t}(\mathrm{n}-1), strictly stronger than g≤t​n\mathrm{g}\leq\mathrm{t}\,\mathrm{n} precisely when t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e}, and reduces Wilf’s conjecture to an inequality free of c\mathrm{c} and n\mathrm{n}. We determine the equality case of g≤t​n\mathrm{g}\leq\mathrm{t}\,\mathrm{n}, recovering a classification of Singhal; answer a question of Moscariello and Sammartano whenever e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1; and correct Kaplan’s classification of the equality case for c≤2​m\mathrm{c}\leq 2\mathrm{m}, from which an infinite family is missing.

Key words and phrases: 
Numerical semigroup, Wilf’s conjecture, pseudo-Frobenius number, type, embedding dimension, Apéry set, Apéry poset, additive basis
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 20M14; Secondary 11D07, 05A20, 11B13

1. Introduction

A numerical semigroup is a submonoid S⊆ℕ={0,1,2,…}S\subseteq\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\} whose complement ℕ∖S\mathbb{N}\setminus S is finite. The elements of ℕ∖S\mathbb{N}\setminus S are the gaps of SS, their number g=g⁡(S)\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{g}(S) is the genus, the largest gap F=F⁡(S)\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{F}(S) is the Frobenius number, and c=c⁡(S)=F+1\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{c}(S)=\mathrm{F}+1 is the conductor. We write

L=L⁡(S)=S∩[0,c),n=n⁡(S)=|L⁡(S)|,\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{L}(S)=S\cap[0,\mathrm{c}),\qquad\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{n}(S)=|\mathrm{L}(S)|,

so that n+g=c\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{c}. Every numerical semigroup has a unique minimal system of generators, whose cardinality e=e⁡(S)\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{e}(S) is the embedding dimension, and we denote by m=m⁡(S)\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{m}(S) the multiplicity, that is, the least positive element of SS. Standard references are the monographs of Rosales and García-Sánchez [20] and of Ramírez Alfonsín [19].

In 1978 Wilf [24] posed a question that remains one of the central open problems in the theory.

Conjecture 1.1 (Wilf).

For every numerical semigroup S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N},

e⁡(S)​n​(S)≥c⁡(S).\mathrm{e}(S)\,\mathrm{n}(S)\;\geq\;\mathrm{c}(S).

We record the discrepancy as the Wilf number

W⁡(S)=e⁡(S)​n​(S)−c⁡(S),\mathrm{W}(S)\;=\;\mathrm{e}(S)\,\mathrm{n}(S)-\mathrm{c}(S),

so that Conjecture 1.1 reads W⁡(S)≥0\mathrm{W}(S)\geq 0.

The conjecture has been established in the following cases: e≤3\mathrm{e}\leq 3, due to Fröberg, Gottlieb and Häggkvist [14] and to Dobbs and Matthews [8]; c≤2​m\mathrm{c}\leq 2\mathrm{m}, due to Kaplan [16]; 2​e≥m2\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{m}, due to Sammartano [21]; c≤3​m\mathrm{c}\leq 3\mathrm{m} and n≤10\mathrm{n}\leq 10, due to Eliahou [9]; 3​e≥m3\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{m}, due to Eliahou [10]; n≤12\mathrm{n}\leq 12, due to Eliahou and Marín-Aragón [13]; semigroups with a large second generator, due to Spirito [23]; semigroups with m|c\mathrm{m}\mid\mathrm{c} and 4​e≥m4\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{m}, due to Eliahou [11]; almost symmetric semigroups, due to Barucci [1] and, by a different route, to D’Anna and Moscariello [4]; multiplicity m≤19\mathrm{m}\leq 19, due to Bruns, García-Sánchez, O’Neill and Wilburne [3] and Kliem and Stump [17]; and genus at most 100100, verified by Delgado, Eliahou and Fromentin [7].

Numerical semigroups with small or negative Wilf number, and the near-misses among them, are studied by Eliahou and Fromentin [12] and by Delgado [5]. Combined with Zhai’s asymptotic count [25], Eliahou’s theorem on c≤3​m\mathrm{c}\leq 3\mathrm{m} shows that the conjecture holds for asymptotically all numerical semigroups ordered by genus. We refer to Delgado’s survey [6] for a systematic account.

1.1. The type and the FGH range

An integer ff is a pseudo-Frobenius number of SS if f∉Sf\notin S and f+s∈Sf+s\in S for every s∈S∖{0}s\in S\setminus\{0\}. The set of these is denoted PF⁡(S)\PF(S) and its cardinality is the type t=t⁡(S)\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{t}(S) of SS. The classical approach to Conjecture 1.1 rests on the inequality of Fröberg, Gottlieb and Häggkvist [14, Theorem 20],

(1) c⁡(S)≤(t⁡(S)+1)​n​(S),\mathrm{c}(S)\;\leq\;\bigl(\mathrm{t}(S)+1\bigr)\,\mathrm{n}(S),

which yields Conjecture 1.1 whenever

(2) t⁡(S)≤e⁡(S)−1.\mathrm{t}(S)\;\leq\;\mathrm{e}(S)-1.

We refer to (2), equivalently to e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1, as the FGH range. It contains all symmetric semigroups and all semigroups of maximal embedding dimension; see [20, Chs. 2–3].

Outside the FGH range, the type has been of limited use. As Delgado observes of (1), “since no upper bound exists for type in higher embedding dimensions, Proposition 3.1 [that is, (1)] cannot yield further general results” [6, §3.1]. Large classes containing many semigroups with t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e} have been settled by other means, almost symmetric semigroups among them. To the best of our knowledge, however, no theorem in the literature takes t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e} as its hypothesis, and none of the known cases of Conjecture 1.1 is proved by an argument that runs through the type in that range. We show that the classical argument behind (1) yields more than the inequality itself, and that the additional structure identifies the obstruction.

1.2. Results

The proof of (1) discards two nonnegative quantities. For an integer x∈[1,F]x\in[1,\mathrm{F}] let νS​(x)=|{f∈PF⁡(S):f−x∈S}|\nu_{S}(x)=|\{f\in\PF(S):f-x\in S\}| be the number of pseudo-Frobenius numbers dominating xx, and set

λS​(y)=|S∩[0,y]|,σ⁡(S)=∑f∈PF⁡(S)|S∩(f,F]|,Θ⁡(S)=∑x∈ℕ∖S(νS​(x)−1).\lambda_{S}(y)=\bigl|S\cap[0,y]\bigr|,\qquad\sigma(S)=\sum_{f\in\PF(S)}\bigl|S\cap(f,\mathrm{F}]\bigr|,\qquad\Theta(S)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{N}\setminus S}\bigl(\nu_{S}(x)-1\bigr).

Here σ⁡(S)\sigma(S), the dominance defect, measures the failure of the pseudo-Frobenius numbers to dominate L⁡(S)\mathrm{L}(S), while Θ⁡(S)\Theta(S), the redundancy defect, measures the redundancy of the covering of the gap set on which the proof of (1) rests. The resulting decomposition of the Wilf number (Proposition 3.2) is exact:

(3) W⁡(S)=(e−t−1)​n+σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S),σ⁡(S),Θ⁡(S)≥ 0,\mathrm{W}(S)\;=\;\bigl(\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{t}-1\bigr)\mathrm{n}\;+\;\sigma(S)\;+\;\Theta(S),\qquad\sigma(S),\ \Theta(S)\ \geq\ 0,

and (1) is what remains once both defects are dropped. Dropping Θ\Theta alone sharpens it to c≤(t+1)​n−σ⁡(S)\mathrm{c}\leq(\mathrm{t}+1)\mathrm{n}-\sigma(S), with equality if and only if Θ⁡(S)=0\Theta(S)=0 (Corollary 3.3).

Our principal result is an upper bound for the type. The invariants occurring in (1) and in Conjecture 1.1 are the two extremal statistics of a single finite poset, the Apéry poset Q(S)=(Ap(S,m)∖{0},⪯S)Q(S)=(\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})\setminus\{0\},\preceq_{S}): its minimal elements are the primitive elements (minimal generators) of SS other than m\mathrm{m}, and its maximal elements are PF⁡(S)+m\PF(S)+\mathrm{m} (Lemma 4.1). The base point need not be the multiplicity: Lemma 4.1 is proved for Ap⁡(S,s)\Ap(S,s) with s∈S∖{0}s\in S\setminus\{0\} arbitrary, giving one inequality for each element of SS (Proposition 4.2); the multiplicity is the unique base point ss for which every minimal element pp satisfies p>sp>s, so that p−sp-s is a gap. Bounding the number of maximal elements by the number of minimal ones then gives the following, in which Ξ⁡(S)=∑w∈Ap⁡(S,m)∖{0}⌊w/m⌋​(νS​(w−m)−1)\Xi(S)=\sum_{w\in\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})\setminus\{0\}}\lfloor w/\mathrm{m}\rfloor(\nu_{S}(w-\mathrm{m})-1).

Theorem 1.2 (cf. Theorem 4.4).

For every numerical semigroup S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N},

t⁡(S)≤∑p∈P∖{m}νS​(p−m)≤e⁡(S)−1+Ξ⁡(S)≤e⁡(S)−1+Θ⁡(S),\mathrm{t}(S)\;\leq\;\sum_{p\in P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}}\nu_{S}(p-\mathrm{m})\;\leq\;\mathrm{e}(S)-1+\Xi(S)\;\leq\;\mathrm{e}(S)-1+\Theta(S),

where PP is the set of primitive elements of SS.

The weighted term Ξ⁡(S)\Xi(S) rests on one further observation: νS\nu_{S} is nondecreasing along the descending chain x,x−m,x−2​m,…x,x-\mathrm{m},x-2\mathrm{m},\dots of gaps (Lemma 4.3), so the redundancy counted by Θ⁡(S)\Theta(S) accumulates at the foot of each residue class. The refinement is strict for all but 24,09424{,}094 of the 23,663,12523{,}663{,}125 numerical semigroups of genus at most 3131. Computation supports the same bound with σ⁡(S)\sigma(S) in place of Ξ⁡(S)\Xi(S) (Conjecture 4.9).

Thus a numerical semigroup lies outside the FGH range only if Θ⁡(S)≥t+1−e\Theta(S)\geq\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e}. Rewritten by means of (3), Theorem 1.2 becomes an unconditional bound for the genus (Corollary 4.8),

g⁡(S)+σ⁡(S)≤e⁡(S)−1+t⁡(S)​(n⁡(S)−1),\mathrm{g}(S)+\sigma(S)\;\leq\;\mathrm{e}(S)-1+\mathrm{t}(S)\bigl(\mathrm{n}(S)-1\bigr),

whose weaker form g≤e−1+t⁡(n−1)\mathrm{g}\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\mathrm{t}(\mathrm{n}-1), obtained by discarding σ\sigma, is strictly stronger than (1) if and only if t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e}, that is, exactly outside the range in which (1) settles Conjecture 1.1.

We do not prove Wilf’s conjecture, and neither bound above settles a case of it that (1) does not: Theorem 1.2 bounds Θ⁡(S)\Theta(S) from below by t+1−e\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e}, whereas by (3) the conjecture requires a bound larger by a factor of n\mathrm{n}.

The same identity does, however, reduce Conjecture 1.1 to a statement in which neither c\mathrm{c} nor n\mathrm{n} appears. Write PF(S)={f1<⋯<ft}\PF(S)=\{f_{1}<\dots<f_{\mathrm{t}}\} and d=t+1−ed=\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e}. Only dd of the t\mathrm{t} nonnegative summands of σ⁡(S)\sigma(S) are needed to absorb the factor n\mathrm{n}, and one obtains unconditionally (Proposition 5.1) that W⁡(S)≥Θ⁡(S)−∑i=1dλS​(fi)\mathrm{W}(S)\geq\Theta(S)-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{S}(f_{i}) whenever t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e}. Wilf’s conjecture therefore follows from the inequality Θ⁡(S)≥∑i=1dλS​(fi)\Theta(S)\geq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{S}(f_{i}) on the range t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e} (Conjecture 5.2 and Proposition 5.3); we verify that inequality over all 171,202,689171{,}202{,}689 numerical semigroups of genus at most 3535.

The equality case W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 was posed by Wilf [24]. Two families are classical: every 22-generated semigroup is symmetric and therefore satisfies W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0; and for m≥2\mathrm{m}\geq 2, k≥1k\geq 1 the semigroup

(4) Tm,k={0,m,2​m,…,(k−1)​m}∪[k​m,∞)=⟨m,k​m+1,k​m+2,…,k​m+m−1⟩T_{\mathrm{m},k}\;=\;\{0,\mathrm{m},2\mathrm{m},\dots,(k-1)\mathrm{m}\}\cup[k\mathrm{m},\infty)\;=\;\langle\mathrm{m},\ k\mathrm{m}+1,\ k\mathrm{m}+2,\ \dots,\ k\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}-1\rangle

has c=k​m\mathrm{c}=k\mathrm{m}, n=k\mathrm{n}=k, e=m\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{m} and W⁡(Tm,k)=0\mathrm{W}(T_{\mathrm{m},k})=0. Moscariello and Sammartano [18, Question 8] asked whether these are the only ones; the question is reproduced as [6, Problem 2.5]. It has been answered affirmatively for c≤3​m\mathrm{c}\leq 3\mathrm{m} [9, Remark 6.6] and, by computation, for m≤15\mathrm{m}\leq 15 [3, Remark 4.7]. We settle it on the whole FGH range.

Theorem 1.3 (cf. Theorem 6.4).

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)+1\mathrm{e}(S)\geq\mathrm{t}(S)+1. Then W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 if and only if e⁡(S)=2\mathrm{e}(S)=2 or S=Tm,kS=T_{\mathrm{m},k} for some m≥3\mathrm{m}\geq 3, k≥1k\geq 1.

The proof shows, via (3), that W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 and e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1 force e=t+1\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}+1 and σ⁡(S)=Θ⁡(S)=0\sigma(S)=\Theta(S)=0, and then classifies the semigroups with σ=Θ=0\sigma=\Theta=0, that is, the equality case of (1). That classification is due to Singhal [22, Theorem 1.6]. The FGH range is a condition on e\mathrm{e} and t\mathrm{t} alone, so Theorem 1.3 imposes no bound on the multiplicity; the theorem covers, for instance, every semigroup of maximal embedding dimension. We conjecture that the hypothesis e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1 can be removed altogether (Conjecture 7.6).

Finally, we correct [16, Proposition 26]. Kaplan proved Wilf’s conjecture for F<2​m\mathrm{F}<2\mathrm{m}, that is, for c≤2​m\mathrm{c}\leq 2\mathrm{m} [16, Theorem 24], and asserted that in this range equality holds only for ⟨m,m+1,…,2​m−1⟩\langle\mathrm{m},\mathrm{m}+1,\dots,2\mathrm{m}-1\rangle and ⟨3,4⟩\langle 3,4\rangle. An infinite family is missing.

Theorem 1.4 (= Theorem 7.3).

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup with c⁡(S)≤2​m​(S)\mathrm{c}(S)\leq 2\mathrm{m}(S). Then W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 if and only if S=Tm,1S=T_{\mathrm{m},1} or S=Tm,2S=T_{\mathrm{m},2} for some m≥2\mathrm{m}\geq 2, or S=⟨3,4⟩S=\langle 3,4\rangle.

The smallest members of the missing family Tm,2=⟨m,2​m+1,…,3​m−1⟩T_{\mathrm{m},2}=\langle\mathrm{m},2\mathrm{m}+1,\dots,3\mathrm{m}-1\rangle are ⟨2,5⟩\langle 2,5\rangle and ⟨3,7,8⟩={0,3}∪[6,∞)\langle 3,7,8\rangle=\{0,3\}\cup[6,\infty); the latter has m=3\mathrm{m}=3, F=5<6=2​m\mathrm{F}=5<6=2\mathrm{m}, n=2\mathrm{n}=2, e=3\mathrm{e}=3 and W=3⋅2−6=0\mathrm{W}=3\cdot 2-6=0. Remark 7.4 identifies the step at which [16, Proposition 26] fails. Our proof of Theorem 1.4 reduces to a statement about perfect additive bases of order 22 (Lemma 7.2).

Sections 4–6 branch from Section 3: Section 4 exploits the redundancy defect, Section 5 the dominance defect, and Section 6, through the identity (3), the vanishing of both. Section 7 is independent of all three, resting only on the elementary Lemma 2.3. Section 8 reports the verification and Section 9 states what remains.

2. Notation and preliminaries

This section fixes notation, records the standard facts used throughout, and computes the invariants of a family of numerical semigroups that recurs below.

Throughout this paper, SS denotes a numerical semigroup and S∗=S∖{0}S^{*}=S\setminus\{0\}. We abbreviate m=m⁡(S)\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{m}(S), F=F⁡(S)\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{F}(S), c=c⁡(S)\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{c}(S), g=g⁡(S)\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{g}(S), L=L⁡(S)\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{L}(S), n=n⁡(S)\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{n}(S), e=e⁡(S)\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{e}(S), t=t⁡(S)\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{t}(S) whenever SS is clear from the context, and we write G⁡(S)=ℕ∖SG(S)=\mathbb{N}\setminus S for the gap set. We exclude S=ℕS=\mathbb{N} throughout, so that m≥2\mathrm{m}\geq 2 and F≥1\mathrm{F}\geq 1. By definition of the conductor, [c,∞)⊆S[\mathrm{c},\infty)\subseteq S.

An element x∈S∗x\in S^{*} is decomposable if x=y+zx=y+z with y,z∈S∗y,z\in S^{*}, and primitive otherwise; the primitive elements form the unique minimal system of generators of SS, so e\mathrm{e} is their number. If x≥c+mx\geq\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{m} then x−m≥cx-\mathrm{m}\geq\mathrm{c}, so x=m+(x−m)x=\mathrm{m}+(x-\mathrm{m}) is decomposable; all primitives therefore lie in [m,c+m)[\mathrm{m},\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{m}).

On ℤ\mathbb{Z} we use the partial order a⪯Sb⇔b−a∈Sa\preceq_{S}b\iff b-a\in S, and we write a≺Sba\prec_{S}b when a⪯Sba\preceq_{S}b and a≠ba\neq b. The following facts are standard; see [20, Ch. 2]. We include proofs of (vii) and of (ii), the latter being used repeatedly below.

Lemma 2.1.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup.

  1. (i)

    PF⁡(S)\PF(S) is precisely the set of maximal elements of (G(S),⪯S)\bigl(G(S),\preceq_{S}\bigr); in particular F∈PF⁡(S)\mathrm{F}\in\PF(S) and t≥1\mathrm{t}\geq 1.

  2. (ii)

    For every x∈G⁡(S)x\in G(S) there exists f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S) with f−x∈Sf-x\in S.

  3. (iii)

    t⁡(S)=1\mathrm{t}(S)=1 if and only if SS is symmetric, that is, g=c/2\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{c}/2.

  4. (iv)

    For every s∈S∗s\in S^{*}, writing Ap⁡(S,s)={u∈S:u−s∉S}\Ap(S,s)=\{u\in S:\ u-s\notin S\} for the Apéry set of SS with respect to ss, one has PF(S)={w−s:wmaximal in (Ap(S,s),⪯S)}\PF(S)=\{w-s:\ w\ \text{maximal in }(\Ap(S,s),\preceq_{S})\}.

  5. (v)

    For every s∈S∗s\in S^{*}, |Ap⁡(S,s)|=s|\Ap(S,s)|=s, and Ap⁡(S,s)\Ap(S,s) contains exactly one element of each residue class modulo ss, namely the least element of SS in that class; in particular 00 is its only element divisible by ss, and s∉Ap⁡(S,s)s\notin\Ap(S,s).

  6. (vi)

    max⁡Ap⁡(S,s)=F+s\max\Ap(S,s)=\mathrm{F}+s for every s∈S∗s\in S^{*}.

  7. (vii)

    e⁡(S)≥2\mathrm{e}(S)\geq 2; and if e⁡(S)=2\mathrm{e}(S)=2 then SS is symmetric.

Proof of (vii) and (ii).

For (vii): if e⁡(S)=1\mathrm{e}(S)=1 then S=⟨m⟩S=\langle\mathrm{m}\rangle, whose complement in ℕ\mathbb{N} is infinite unless m=1\mathrm{m}=1, that is, unless S=ℕS=\mathbb{N}. The symmetry of S=⟨a,b⟩S=\langle a,b\rangle with gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1 is Sylvester’s classical computation of F=a​b−a−b\mathrm{F}=ab-a-b and g=(a−1)​(b−1)/2\mathrm{g}=(a-1)(b-1)/2; see [19, Ch. 3].

For (ii), let x∈G⁡(S)x\in G(S) and let Y={y∈G⁡(S):y−x∈S}Y=\{y\in G(S):\ y-x\in S\}. Then x∈Yx\in Y, so Y≠∅Y\neq\emptyset, and YY is finite because Y⊆G⁡(S)Y\subseteq G(S). Let f=max⁡Yf=\max Y. If s∈S∗s\in S^{*} and f+s∉Sf+s\notin S, then f+s∈G⁡(S)f+s\in G(S) and (f+s)−x=(f−x)+s∈S(f+s)-x=(f-x)+s\in S, so f+s∈Yf+s\in Y, contradicting maximality. Thus ff is a maximal element of (G(S),⪯S)(G(S),\preceq_{S}); by (i), f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S), and f−x∈Sf-x\in S. ∎

The decomposition of the next section counts the incidences between pseudo-Frobenius numbers and elements of SS. We record the two properties of that incidence set which the count requires.

Lemma 2.2.

Let Π={(f,s)∈PF⁡(S)×S:s≤f}\Pi=\{(f,s)\in\PF(S)\times S:\ s\leq f\}.

  1. (i)

    For every (f,s)∈Π(f,s)\in\Pi one has f−s∈G⁡(S)f-s\in G(S).

  2. (ii)

    The map π:Π→G⁡(S)\pi:\Pi\to G(S), π⁡(f,s)=f−s\pi(f,s)=f-s, is surjective.

Proof.

(i) If s=0s=0 then f−s=f∈G⁡(S)f-s=f\in G(S). If s>0s>0 and f−s∈Sf-s\in S, then f=(f−s)+s∈Sf=(f-s)+s\in S, contradicting f∈G⁡(S)f\in G(S). (ii) is Lemma 2.1(ii). ∎

Finally we record the invariants of the family (4).

Lemma 2.3.

Let m≥2\mathrm{m}\geq 2 and k≥1k\geq 1, and let Tm,k={0,m,…,(k−1)​m}∪[k​m,∞)T_{\mathrm{m},k}=\{0,\mathrm{m},\dots,(k-1)\mathrm{m}\}\cup[k\mathrm{m},\infty). Then Tm,kT_{\mathrm{m},k} is a numerical semigroup with

m⁡(Tm,k)=m,c=k​m,n=k,e=m,t=m−1,W⁡(Tm,k)=0,\mathrm{m}(T_{\mathrm{m},k})=\mathrm{m},\quad\mathrm{c}=k\mathrm{m},\quad\mathrm{n}=k,\quad\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{m},\quad\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{m}-1,\quad\mathrm{W}(T_{\mathrm{m},k})=0,

and Tm,k=⟨m,k​m+1,k​m+2,…,k​m+m−1⟩T_{\mathrm{m},k}=\langle\mathrm{m},\,k\mathrm{m}+1,\,k\mathrm{m}+2,\dots,k\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}-1\rangle.

Proof.

Closure under addition is clear: a sum of two multiples of m\mathrm{m} that is less than k​mk\mathrm{m} is again such a multiple, and any sum involving an element ≥k​m\geq k\mathrm{m} is ≥k​m\geq k\mathrm{m}. As k​mk\mathrm{m} and k​m+1k\mathrm{m}+1 both belong to Tm,kT_{\mathrm{m},k}, the set generates ℤ\mathbb{Z}, so Tm,kT_{\mathrm{m},k} is a numerical semigroup; its least positive element is m\mathrm{m}, and k​m−1∉Tm,kk\mathrm{m}-1\notin T_{\mathrm{m},k} because m≥2\mathrm{m}\geq 2, whence c=k​m\mathrm{c}=k\mathrm{m} and L={0,m,…,(k−1)​m}\mathrm{L}=\{0,\mathrm{m},\dots,(k-1)\mathrm{m}\} has kk elements.

We determine the primitives. Every x≥k​m+mx\geq k\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m} is decomposable, since x=m+(x−m)x=\mathrm{m}+(x-\mathrm{m}) with x−m≥k​mx-\mathrm{m}\geq k\mathrm{m}. Let x=k​m+rx=k\mathrm{m}+r with 0≤r<m0\leq r<\mathrm{m} and suppose x=a+bx=a+b with a,b∈Tm,k∗a,b\in T_{\mathrm{m},k}^{*}. If both a,b<k​ma,b<k\mathrm{m} then both are multiples of m\mathrm{m}, so m|x\mathrm{m}\mid x and hence r=0r=0; if instead a≥k​ma\geq k\mathrm{m}, then x=a+b≥k​m+mx=a+b\geq k\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}, a contradiction. Thus the only element of [km,km+m)[k\mathrm{m},k\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}) that can be decomposable is k​mk\mathrm{m} itself, which is decomposable exactly when k≥2k\geq 2 (as k​m=m+(k−1)​mk\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{m}+(k-1)\mathrm{m}). Among the elements i​mi\mathrm{m} with 1≤i≤k−11\leq i\leq k-1, those with i≥2i\geq 2 are decomposable and m\mathrm{m} is not. Hence the primitives are m\mathrm{m} together with k​m+1,…,k​m+m−1k\mathrm{m}+1,\dots,k\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}-1, so e=m\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{m}.

For the type, the gaps of Tm,kT_{\mathrm{m},k} are exactly the integers i​m+ji\mathrm{m}+j with 0≤i≤k−10\leq i\leq k-1 and 1≤j≤m−11\leq j\leq\mathrm{m}-1. If i=k−1i=k-1, then for every s∈Tm,k∗s\in T_{\mathrm{m},k}^{*} we have s≥ms\geq\mathrm{m} and therefore (k−1)​m+j+s≥k​m+j>k​m(k-1)\mathrm{m}+j+s\geq k\mathrm{m}+j>k\mathrm{m}, so (k−1)​m+j∈PF⁡(Tm,k)(k-1)\mathrm{m}+j\in\PF(T_{\mathrm{m},k}). If i≤k−2i\leq k-2, then (i​m+j)+m=(i+1)​m+j(i\mathrm{m}+j)+\mathrm{m}=(i+1)\mathrm{m}+j with i+1≤k−1i+1\leq k-1 and 1≤j≤m−11\leq j\leq\mathrm{m}-1, which is again a gap, so i​m+j∉PF⁡(Tm,k)i\mathrm{m}+j\notin\PF(T_{\mathrm{m},k}). Hence PF⁡(Tm,k)={(k−1)​m+j:1≤j≤m−1}\PF(T_{\mathrm{m},k})=\{(k-1)\mathrm{m}+j:1\leq j\leq\mathrm{m}-1\}, so t=m−1\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{m}-1 and W=m⋅k−k​m=0\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{m}\cdot k-k\mathrm{m}=0. ∎

For m=2\mathrm{m}=2 the family degenerates to T2,k=⟨2,2​k+1⟩T_{2,k}=\langle 2,2k+1\rangle, which is 22-generated and hence symmetric; this is why the case m=2\mathrm{m}=2 is absorbed into the symmetric case in the classifications proved below.

3. A defect decomposition of the Wilf number

The Fröberg–Gottlieb–Häggkvist argument bounds the genus by covering the gap set with the reflected sets f−Lf-\mathrm{L}, f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S), and discarding two sources of loss: the elements of L\mathrm{L} that exceed a given pseudo-Frobenius number, and the gaps that the covering reaches more than once. Restoring both turns (1) into an identity for the Wilf number.

Definition 3.1.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup. For y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z} set λS​(y)=|S∩[0,y]|\lambda_{S}(y)=\bigl|S\cap[0,y]\bigr|, and for every integer x∈[1,F]x\in[1,\mathrm{F}] set

νS​(x)=|{f∈PF⁡(S):f−x∈S}|.\nu_{S}(x)=\bigl|\{f\in\PF(S):\ f-x\in S\}\bigr|.

Define

Λ⁡(S)=∑f∈PF⁡(S)λS​(f),σ⁡(S)=∑f∈PF⁡(S)|S∩(f,F]|,Θ⁡(S)=∑x∈G⁡(S)(νS​(x)−1),\Lambda(S)=\sum_{f\in\PF(S)}\lambda_{S}(f),\qquad\sigma(S)=\sum_{f\in\PF(S)}\bigl|S\cap(f,\mathrm{F}]\bigr|,\qquad\Theta(S)=\sum_{x\in G(S)}\bigl(\nu_{S}(x)-1\bigr),

and call σ⁡(S)\sigma(S) the dominance defect and Θ⁡(S)\Theta(S) the redundancy defect of SS.

By Lemma 2.2(i) one has νS​(x)=0\nu_{S}(x)=0 for x∈S∩[1,F]x\in S\cap[1,\mathrm{F}], and by Lemma 2.1(ii) one has νS​(x)≥1\nu_{S}(x)\geq 1 for x∈G⁡(S)x\in G(S); hence Θ⁡(S)≥0\Theta(S)\geq 0.

Since PF⁡(S)⊆[1,F]\PF(S)\subseteq[1,\mathrm{F}] and S∩[0,f]⊆LS\cap[0,f]\subseteq\mathrm{L} for f≤Ff\leq\mathrm{F}, we have λS​(f)=|L∩[0,f]|≤n\lambda_{S}(f)=\bigl|\mathrm{L}\cap[0,f]\bigr|\leq\mathrm{n} for every f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S), and therefore

(5) σ⁡(S)=∑f∈PF⁡(S)(n−λS​(f))=t​n−Λ⁡(S)≥ 0,\sigma(S)=\sum_{f\in\PF(S)}\bigl(\mathrm{n}-\lambda_{S}(f)\bigr)=\mathrm{t}\,\mathrm{n}-\Lambda(S)\ \geq\ 0,

the middle equality because S∩[0,f]S\cap[0,f] and S∩(f,F]S\cap(f,\mathrm{F}] partition S∩[0,F]=LS\cap[0,\mathrm{F}]=\mathrm{L} for f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S).

Proposition 3.2 (Defect decomposition).

For every numerical semigroup S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N},

(6) g⁡(S)=Λ⁡(S)−Θ⁡(S),\mathrm{g}(S)\;=\;\Lambda(S)-\Theta(S),

and consequently

(7) W⁡(S)=(e⁡(S)−t⁡(S)−1)​n​(S)+σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S).\mathrm{W}(S)\;=\;\bigl(\mathrm{e}(S)-\mathrm{t}(S)-1\bigr)\,\mathrm{n}(S)\;+\;\sigma(S)\;+\;\Theta(S).
Proof.

Let Π\Pi be as in Lemma 2.2; it is finite. Counting Π\Pi by its first coordinate gives |Π|=∑f∈PF⁡(S)|S∩[0,f]|=Λ⁡(S)|\Pi|=\sum_{f\in\PF(S)}\bigl|S\cap[0,f]\bigr|=\Lambda(S). By Lemma 2.2 the map π:Π→G⁡(S)\pi:\Pi\to G(S), π⁡(f,s)=f−s\pi(f,s)=f-s, is well defined and surjective. Its fibre over a gap xx is {(f,f−x):f∈PF(S),f−x∈S}\{(f,f-x):\ f\in\PF(S),\ f-x\in S\}: a pair (f,s)∈Π(f,s)\in\Pi satisfies f−s=xf-s=x if and only if s=f−xs=f-x, and then 0≤s≤f0\leq s\leq f automatically since x≥1x\geq 1. As 1≤x≤F1\leq x\leq\mathrm{F}, that fibre has cardinality νS​(x)\nu_{S}(x). Hence

Λ⁡(S)=|Π|=∑x∈G⁡(S)νS​(x)=g⁡(S)+∑x∈G⁡(S)(νS​(x)−1)=g⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S),\Lambda(S)=|\Pi|=\sum_{x\in G(S)}\nu_{S}(x)=\mathrm{g}(S)+\sum_{x\in G(S)}\bigl(\nu_{S}(x)-1\bigr)=\mathrm{g}(S)+\Theta(S),

which is (6). For (7), use c=n+g\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{g} and (5):

W⁡(S)=e​n−c=e​n−n−g=(e−1)​n−Λ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)=(e−1)​n−(t​n−σ⁡(S))+Θ⁡(S),\mathrm{W}(S)=\mathrm{e}\,\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{e}\,\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{n}-\mathrm{g}=(\mathrm{e}-1)\mathrm{n}-\Lambda(S)+\Theta(S)=(\mathrm{e}-1)\mathrm{n}-\bigl(\mathrm{t}\,\mathrm{n}-\sigma(S)\bigr)+\Theta(S),

Corollary 3.3.

For every numerical semigroup S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N},

(8) c⁡(S)≤(t⁡(S)+1)​n​(S)−σ⁡(S)≤(t⁡(S)+1)​n​(S).\mathrm{c}(S)\;\leq\;\bigl(\mathrm{t}(S)+1\bigr)\mathrm{n}(S)-\sigma(S)\;\leq\;\bigl(\mathrm{t}(S)+1\bigr)\mathrm{n}(S).

Proof.

By (6) and (5), c=n+g=n+Λ−Θ=(t+1)​n−σ−Θ\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{n}+\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{n}+\Lambda-\Theta=(\mathrm{t}+1)\mathrm{n}-\sigma-\Theta, and both σ\sigma and Θ\Theta are nonnegative. ∎

The outer inequality in (8) is (1), equivalently g≤t​n\mathrm{g}\leq\mathrm{t}\,\mathrm{n}; the first inequality strictly refines it whenever σ⁡(S)>0\sigma(S)>0. Explicitly, (6) and (5) say that

(9) g⁡(S)≤Λ⁡(S)≤t⁡(S)​n​(S),Θ⁡(S)=Λ⁡(S)−g⁡(S),σ⁡(S)=t⁡(S)​n​(S)−Λ⁡(S).\mathrm{g}(S)\;\leq\;\Lambda(S)\;\leq\;\mathrm{t}(S)\,\mathrm{n}(S),\qquad\Theta(S)=\Lambda(S)-\mathrm{g}(S),\quad\sigma(S)=\mathrm{t}(S)\,\mathrm{n}(S)-\Lambda(S).

The lower bound is the surjectivity of π\pi, and the upper bound is λS​(f)≤n\lambda_{S}(f)\leq\mathrm{n}; (1) is their combination. The defects σ\sigma and Θ\Theta measure distinct phenomena: σ⁡(S)=0\sigma(S)=0 says that every pseudo-Frobenius number exceeds all elements of L⁡(S)\mathrm{L}(S), whereas Θ⁡(S)=0\Theta(S)=0 says that the covering of G⁡(S)G(S) furnished by Lemma 2.1(ii) is a partition.

Example 3.4.

4. The Apéry poset and an upper bound for the type

Throughout this section we write

Q(S)=(Ap(S,m)∖{0},⪯S),Q(S)\;=\;\bigl(\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})\setminus\{0\},\ \preceq_{S}\bigr),

the Apéry poset of SS, which has m−1\mathrm{m}-1 elements. Its maximal elements number t\mathrm{t} and its minimal elements e−1\mathrm{e}-1, so the passage from t\mathrm{t} to e−1\mathrm{e}-1 is a poset-theoretic estimate, whose loss the section bounds.

The construction does not single out the multiplicity. We therefore define the poset for an arbitrary base point: for s∈S∗s\in S^{*} write Qs(S)=(Ap(S,s)∖{0},⪯S)Q_{s}(S)=\bigl(\Ap(S,s)\setminus\{0\},\preceq_{S}\bigr), so that Q​(S)=Qm​(S)Q(S)=Q_{\mathrm{m}}(S). For s=ms=\mathrm{m} both descriptions below are standard, that of Max⁡Q⁡(S)\Max Q(S) being Lemma 2.1(iv) and that of Min⁡Q⁡(S)\Min Q(S) the usual passage from the Apéry set to the minimal system of generators, see [20, Ch. 2]; since the general base point costs nothing and the two are used jointly, we prove them together.

Lemma 4.1.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup, let PP be its set of primitive elements, and let s∈S∗s\in S^{*}. Then

MinQs(S)={p∈P:p≠s,p−s∉S},MaxQs(S)=PF(S)+s,\Min Q_{s}(S)=\{p\in P:\ p\neq s,\ p-s\notin S\},\qquad\Max Q_{s}(S)=\PF(S)+s,

where Min\Min and Max\Max denote the sets of minimal and of maximal elements. For s=ms=\mathrm{m} this reads

Min⁡Q⁡(S)=P∖{m},Max⁡Q⁡(S)=PF⁡(S)+m,\Min Q(S)=P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\},\qquad\Max Q(S)=\PF(S)+\mathrm{m},

so that |Min⁡Q⁡(S)|=e⁡(S)−1|\Min Q(S)|=\mathrm{e}(S)-1 and |Max⁡Q⁡(S)|=t⁡(S)|\Max Q(S)|=\mathrm{t}(S).

Proof.

A primitive pp with p≠sp\neq s and p−s∉Sp-s\notin S lies in Ap⁡(S,s)\Ap(S,s) by definition, and p≠0p\neq 0; and s∉Ap⁡(S,s)s\notin\Ap(S,s) by Lemma 2.1(v). So the displayed set is contained in Ap⁡(S,s)∖{0}\Ap(S,s)\setminus\{0\}.

Let w∈Ap⁡(S,s)∖{0}w\in\Ap(S,s)\setminus\{0\}. If ww is decomposable, write w=x+yw=x+y with x,y∈S∗x,y\in S^{*}. Not both xx and yy are divisible by ss: otherwise s|ws\mid w, whereas by Lemma 2.1(v) the only element of Ap⁡(S,s)\Ap(S,s) divisible by ss is 00. Say s∤xs\nmid x, and let x′x^{\prime} be the element of Ap⁡(S,s)\Ap(S,s) congruent to xx modulo ss; by Lemma 2.1(v) it is the least element of SS in that class, so x′≤xx^{\prime}\leq x, and x′≠0x^{\prime}\neq 0 since s∤xs\nmid x. Then w−x′=(x−x′)+y∈Sw-x^{\prime}=(x-x^{\prime})+y\in S, because x−x′x-x^{\prime} is a nonnegative multiple of ss and y∈Sy\in S; moreover w−x′≥y>0w-x^{\prime}\geq y>0, so x′≺Swx^{\prime}\prec_{S}w and ww is not minimal in Qs​(S)Q_{s}(S). Conversely, if ww is not minimal, then w=z+(w−z)w=z+(w-z) for some z∈Ap⁡(S,s)∖{0}z\in\Ap(S,s)\setminus\{0\} with w−z∈S∗w-z\in S^{*}, so ww is decomposable. Hence the minimal elements of Qs​(S)Q_{s}(S) are exactly the primitive elements lying in Ap⁡(S,s)∖{0}\Ap(S,s)\setminus\{0\}, which is the asserted set.

The description of Max⁡Qs​(S)\Max Q_{s}(S) is Lemma 2.1(iv); and 00 is not maximal, since s≥m≥2s\geq\mathrm{m}\geq 2 forces Ap⁡(S,s)≠{0}\Ap(S,s)\neq\{0\} and 0⪯Sw0\preceq_{S}w for every ww. Finally, for s=ms=\mathrm{m} every primitive p≠mp\neq\mathrm{m} satisfies p−m∉Sp-\mathrm{m}\notin S, since otherwise p=m+(p−m)p=\mathrm{m}+(p-\mathrm{m}) would be decomposable; so Min⁡Q⁡(S)=P∖{m}\Min Q(S)=P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}, a set of e−1\mathrm{e}-1 elements. ∎

Bounding the number of maximal elements of Qs​(S)Q_{s}(S) by the number of its minimal ones gives one inequality for every base point.

Proposition 4.2.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup. For every s∈S∗s\in S^{*},

(10) t⁡(S)≤∑p∈Min⁡Qs​(S)|{f∈PF⁡(S):f+s−p∈S}|.\mathrm{t}(S)\;\leq\;\sum_{p\in\Min Q_{s}(S)}\bigl|\{f\in\PF(S):\ f+s-p\in S\}\bigr|.
Proof.

The poset Qs​(S)Q_{s}(S) is finite and nonempty, since |Ap⁡(S,s)|=s≥m≥2|\Ap(S,s)|=s\geq\mathrm{m}\geq 2 by Lemma 2.1(v); hence Min⁡Qs​(S)≠∅\Min Q_{s}(S)\neq\emptyset. Every element of a finite poset lies above at least one minimal element, so we may choose, for each w∈Max⁡Qs​(S)w\in\Max Q_{s}(S), an element μ⁡(w)∈Min⁡Qs​(S)\mu(w)\in\Min Q_{s}(S) with μ(w)⪯Sw\mu(w)\preceq_{S}w. Counting the fibres of μ\mu,

t(S)=|MaxQs(S)|=∑q∈Min⁡Qs​(S)|μ−1(q)|≤∑q∈Min⁡Qs​(S)|{w∈MaxQs(S):q⪯Sw}|,\mathrm{t}(S)=\bigl|\Max Q_{s}(S)\bigr|=\sum_{q\in\Min Q_{s}(S)}\bigl|\mu^{-1}(q)\bigr|\;\leq\;\sum_{q\in\Min Q_{s}(S)}\bigl|\{w\in\Max Q_{s}(S):\ q\preceq_{S}w\}\bigr|,

using |Max⁡Qs​(S)|=t⁡(S)|\Max Q_{s}(S)|=\mathrm{t}(S) from Lemma 4.1. For p∈Min⁡Qs​(S)p\in\Min Q_{s}(S) the same lemma gives {w∈MaxQs(S):p⪯Sw}={f+s:f∈PF(S),f+s−p∈S}\{w\in\Max Q_{s}(S):p\preceq_{S}w\}=\{f+s:\ f\in\PF(S),\ f+s-p\in S\}, whose cardinality is the pp-th summand of (10). ∎

The base point s=ms=\mathrm{m} is distinguished: it is the only one for which every minimal element pp of Qs​(S)Q_{s}(S) satisfies p>sp>s, since for s≠ms\neq\mathrm{m} the multiplicity itself lies in Min⁡Qs​(S)\Min Q_{s}(S) and is smaller than ss. For s=ms=\mathrm{m}, therefore, p−sp-s is a gap, the summands of (10) become values of νS\nu_{S}, and (10) becomes a bound by the redundancy defect. Less than Θ⁡(S)\Theta(S) is needed, by the following monotonicity.

Lemma 4.3.

Let x∈G⁡(S)x\in G(S) and s∈Ss\in S with x−s≥1x-s\geq 1. Then x−s∈G⁡(S)x-s\in G(S) and νS​(x−s)≥νS​(x)\nu_{S}(x-s)\geq\nu_{S}(x).

Proof.

If x−sx-s lay in SS then x=(x−s)+sx=(x-s)+s would lie in SS, so x−sx-s is a gap. If f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S) satisfies f−x∈Sf-x\in S, then f−(x−s)=(f−x)+s∈Sf-(x-s)=(f-x)+s\in S; thus every pseudo-Frobenius number counted by νS​(x)\nu_{S}(x) is counted by νS​(x−s)\nu_{S}(x-s). ∎

The monotonicity of Lemma 4.3 lets one weight each element ww of the Apéry set by the number ⌊w/m⌋\lfloor w/\mathrm{m}\rfloor of gaps below it in its residue class.

Theorem 4.4.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup, let PP be its set of primitive elements, and put

(11) Ξ⁡(S)=∑w∈Ap⁡(S,m)∖{0}⌊wm⌋​(νS​(w−m)−1).\Xi(S)\;=\;\sum_{w\in\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})\setminus\{0\}}\Bigl\lfloor\tfrac{w}{\mathrm{m}}\Bigr\rfloor\bigl(\nu_{S}(w-\mathrm{m})-1\bigr).

Then

(12) t⁡(S)≤∑p∈P∖{m}νS​(p−m)≤e⁡(S)−1+Ξ⁡(S)≤e⁡(S)−1+Θ⁡(S).\mathrm{t}(S)\;\leq\;\sum_{p\in P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}}\nu_{S}(p-\mathrm{m})\;\leq\;\mathrm{e}(S)-1+\Xi(S)\;\leq\;\mathrm{e}(S)-1+\Theta(S).
Proof.

Take s=ms=\mathrm{m} in Proposition 4.2. By Lemma 4.1, Min⁡Q⁡(S)=P∖{m}\Min Q(S)=P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}, and for such a pp one has p−m∉Sp-\mathrm{m}\notin S and p>mp>\mathrm{m}, since p∈S∗p\in S^{*} forces p≥mp\geq\mathrm{m} while p≠mp\neq\mathrm{m}. As max⁡Ap⁡(S,m)=F+m\max\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})=\mathrm{F}+\mathrm{m} by Lemma 2.1(vi), we get 1≤p−m≤F1\leq p-\mathrm{m}\leq\mathrm{F}, so p−mp-\mathrm{m} is a gap of SS, and

p⪯Sf+m⇔f+m−p∈S⇔f−(p−m)∈S.p\preceq_{S}f+\mathrm{m}\iff f+\mathrm{m}-p\in S\iff f-(p-\mathrm{m})\in S.

Hence the pp-th summand of (10) equals νS​(p−m)\nu_{S}(p-\mathrm{m}), which is the first inequality in (12).

For the third, fix w∈Ap⁡(S,m)∖{0}w\in\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})\setminus\{0\} and put k=⌊w/m⌋k=\lfloor w/\mathrm{m}\rfloor. By Lemma 2.1(v), m∤w\mathrm{m}\nmid w and ww is the least element of SS in its class modulo m\mathrm{m}; hence w−m,w−2​m,…,w−k​mw-\mathrm{m},w-2\mathrm{m},\dots,w-k\mathrm{m} are kk distinct gaps of SS, and by Lemma 4.3, νS​(w−j​m)≥νS​(w−m)\nu_{S}(w-j\mathrm{m})\geq\nu_{S}(w-\mathrm{m}) for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k. Distinct ww give gaps in distinct residue classes, and every gap arises this way, so

Θ⁡(S)=∑x∈G⁡(S)(νS​(x)−1)≥∑w∈Ap⁡(S,m)∖{0}kw​(νS​(w−m)−1)=Ξ⁡(S),\Theta(S)=\sum_{x\in G(S)}\bigl(\nu_{S}(x)-1\bigr)\;\geq\;\sum_{w\in\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})\setminus\{0\}}k_{w}\bigl(\nu_{S}(w-\mathrm{m})-1\bigr)=\Xi(S),

where kw=⌊w/m⌋k_{w}=\lfloor w/\mathrm{m}\rfloor; this is the third inequality. For the second, P∖{m}⊆Ap⁡(S,m)∖{0}P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}\subseteq\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})\setminus\{0\} and kp≥1k_{p}\geq 1 for such pp, while all summands in (11) are nonnegative, so

∑p∈P∖{m}νS​(p−m)=(e−1)+∑p∈P∖{m}(νS​(p−m)−1)≤(e−1)+Ξ⁡(S).\sum_{p\in P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}}\nu_{S}(p-\mathrm{m})=(\mathrm{e}-1)+\sum_{p\in P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}}\bigl(\nu_{S}(p-\mathrm{m})-1\bigr)\leq(\mathrm{e}-1)+\Xi(S).

∎

Theorem 4.4 makes Ξ⁡(S)\Xi(S), and a fortiori Θ⁡(S)\Theta(S), the necessary cost of leaving the FGH range: t>e−1\mathrm{t}>\mathrm{e}-1 forces Ξ⁡(S)≥t+1−e\Xi(S)\geq\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e}. The converse fails: both quantities may be large while SS lies well inside the FGH range.

Example 4.5.

Let S={0}∪[15,23]∪[30,∞)S=\{0\}\cup[15,23]\cup[30,\infty). Corollary 4.8.

For every numerical semigroup S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N},

5. A reduction of Wilf’s conjecture

The argument of this section uses only the identity (7) and is independent of Section 4. By (7), Conjecture 1.1 is immediate when t≤e−1\mathrm{t}\leq\mathrm{e}-1 and is otherwise equivalent to the lower bound σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)≥(t+1−e)​n\sigma(S)+\Theta(S)\geq\bigl(\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e}\bigr)\mathrm{n}, whose right-hand side grows with n\mathrm{n}. The dominance defect is a sum of t\mathrm{t} nonnegative terms, and only t+1−e\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e} of them are needed to absorb that growth.

Proposition 5.1.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup with t⁡(S)≥e⁡(S)\mathrm{t}(S)\geq\mathrm{e}(S), write PF(S)={f1<f2<⋯<ft}\PF(S)=\{f_{1}<f_{2}<\dots<f_{\mathrm{t}}\} and put d=t⁡(S)+1−e⁡(S)≥1d=\mathrm{t}(S)+1-\mathrm{e}(S)\geq 1. Then

(14) W⁡(S)≥Θ⁡(S)−∑i=1dλS​(fi).\mathrm{W}(S)\;\geq\;\Theta(S)\;-\;\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{S}(f_{i}).
Proof.

By (5), σ⁡(S)=∑i=1t(n−λS​(fi))\sigma(S)=\sum_{i=1}^{\mathrm{t}}\bigl(\mathrm{n}-\lambda_{S}(f_{i})\bigr), and every summand is nonnegative because λS​(f)≤n\lambda_{S}(f)\leq\mathrm{n} for f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S). As e≥1\mathrm{e}\geq 1 we have d≤td\leq\mathrm{t}, so discarding all but the first dd summands gives

σ⁡(S)≥∑i=1d(n−λS​(fi))=d​n−∑i=1dλS​(fi).\sigma(S)\;\geq\;\sum_{i=1}^{d}\bigl(\mathrm{n}-\lambda_{S}(f_{i})\bigr)\;=\;d\,\mathrm{n}-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{S}(f_{i}).

The first term of (7) is (e−t−1)​n=−d​n(\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{t}-1)\mathrm{n}=-d\,\mathrm{n}, so W⁡(S)=−d​n+σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)≥Θ⁡(S)−∑i=1dλS​(fi)\mathrm{W}(S)=-d\,\mathrm{n}+\sigma(S)+\Theta(S)\geq\Theta(S)-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{S}(f_{i}). ∎

Since λS\lambda_{S} is nondecreasing, retaining the dd smallest pseudo-Frobenius numbers gives the strongest inequality of this shape. In (14) the conductor and n\mathrm{n} have disappeared, and the number of terms subtracted is governed by how far SS lies outside the FGH range. The following statement asserts that its right-hand side is nonnegative.

Conjecture 5.2.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup with t⁡(S)≥e⁡(S)\mathrm{t}(S)\geq\mathrm{e}(S), write PF(S)={f1<⋯<ft}\PF(S)=\{f_{1}<\dots<f_{\mathrm{t}}\} and put d=t⁡(S)+1−e⁡(S)d=\mathrm{t}(S)+1-\mathrm{e}(S). Then

Θ⁡(S)≥∑i=1dλS​(fi).\Theta(S)\;\geq\;\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{S}(f_{i}).
Proposition 5.3.

Conjecture 5.2 implies Conjecture 1.1.

Proof.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N}. If t⁡(S)≤e⁡(S)−1\mathrm{t}(S)\leq\mathrm{e}(S)-1 then W⁡(S)≥0\mathrm{W}(S)\geq 0 by Corollary 3.3. Otherwise Conjecture 5.2 applies and (14) gives W⁡(S)≥0\mathrm{W}(S)\geq 0. ∎

The case d=1d=1, that is t=e\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{e}, is the first one the Fröberg–Gottlieb–Häggkvist inequality fails to cover; there (14) reads W⁡(S)≥Θ⁡(S)−λS​(f1)\mathrm{W}(S)\geq\Theta(S)-\lambda_{S}(f_{1}), so Wilf’s conjecture holds for every numerical semigroup with t=e\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{e} whose least pseudo-Frobenius number satisfies λS​(f1)≤Θ⁡(S)\lambda_{S}(f_{1})\leq\Theta(S).

Remark 5.4.

Conjecture 5.2 is not a weakening of Conjecture 1.1. On the range t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e} the latter is equivalent, by (7) and (5), to

Θ⁡(S)≥∑i=1tλS​(fi)−(t−d)​n,\Theta(S)\;\geq\;\sum_{i=1}^{\mathrm{t}}\lambda_{S}(f_{i})\;-\;(\mathrm{t}-d)\,\mathrm{n},

and the difference between this right-hand side and that of Conjecture 5.2 is ∑i=d+1t(n−λS​(fi))≥0\sum_{i=d+1}^{\mathrm{t}}\bigl(\mathrm{n}-\lambda_{S}(f_{i})\bigr)\geq 0. The inequality of Conjecture 5.2 is therefore pointwise at least as strong, and strictly stronger whenever λS​(fi)<n\lambda_{S}(f_{i})<\mathrm{n} for some i>di>d; a proof of it would be a proof of Conjecture 1.1, not a step towards one. The reduction changes the shape of the problem, not its difficulty: Conjecture 5.2 relates the redundancy defect to the pseudo-Frobenius numbers alone, with neither of the global invariants c\mathrm{c} and n\mathrm{n} appearing; and, unlike Conjecture 1.1, it is not tight in the range we have computed.

6. The equality case

The equality case of (1) was determined by Singhal [22, Theorem 1.6], in the equivalent form t=g/(F+1−g)\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{g}/(\mathrm{F}+1-\mathrm{g}) and without reference to Wilf’s conjecture. We give an independent proof, in the formulation that the equality case of Wilf’s conjecture requires: the hypothesis is σ⁡(S)=Θ⁡(S)=0\sigma(S)=\Theta(S)=0, which is the condition (7) produces. We then settle that case throughout the FGH range. Both rest on a description of the semigroups with σ=Θ=0\sigma=\Theta=0, which pins down PF⁡(S)\PF(S) and the spacing of L⁡(S)\mathrm{L}(S). The first half of that description needs only σ=0\sigma=0: it shows that PF⁡(S)\PF(S) always contains the final run of gaps [ℓ+1,F][\ell+1,\mathrm{F}], and that σ⁡(S)\sigma(S) vanishes precisely when it contains nothing else.

Lemma 6.1.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup, put ℓ=max⁡L⁡(S)\ell=\max\mathrm{L}(S) and K=F−ℓK=\mathrm{F}-\ell. Then:

For s∈S∗s\in S^{*} we have s≥m≥K+1s\geq\mathrm{m}\geq K+1 by (i), so x+s≥ℓ+1+K+1=F+2>Fx+s\geq\ell+1+K+1=\mathrm{F}+2>\mathrm{F}, whence x+s≥cx+s\geq\mathrm{c} and x+s∈Sx+s\in S. Thus x∈PF⁡(S)x\in\PF(S).

(iii) Let f∈PF⁡(S)f\in\PF(S). Then f≠ℓf\neq\ell, since ℓ∈S\ell\in S. If f<ℓf<\ell then ℓ∈S∩(f,F]\ell\in S\cap(f,\mathrm{F}], so that term contributes at least 11 to σ⁡(S)\sigma(S); if f>ℓf>\ell then S∩(f,F]⊆S∩(ℓ,c)=∅S\cap(f,\mathrm{F}]\subseteq S\cap(\ell,\mathrm{c})=\emptyset and the term vanishes. Finally F=ℓ+t=nm−1\mathrm{F}=\ell+\mathrm{t}=\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}-1, so c=nm\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m} and S=L∪[c,∞)=Tm,nS=\mathrm{L}\cup[\mathrm{c},\infty)=T_{\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}}. ∎

Theorem 6.4.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)+1\mathrm{e}(S)\geq\mathrm{t}(S)+1. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0;

  2. (ii)

    e⁡(S)=t⁡(S)+1\mathrm{e}(S)=\mathrm{t}(S)+1 and c⁡(S)=(t⁡(S)+1)​n​(S)\mathrm{c}(S)=(\mathrm{t}(S)+1)\mathrm{n}(S);

  3. (iii)

    e⁡(S)=2\mathrm{e}(S)=2, or S=Tm,kS=T_{\mathrm{m},k} for some m≥3\mathrm{m}\geq 3, k≥1k\geq 1.

Proof.

(i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii). By (7), 0=W⁡(S)=(e−t−1)​n+σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)0=\mathrm{W}(S)=(\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{t}-1)\mathrm{n}+\sigma(S)+\Theta(S). All three summands are nonnegative, the first because e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1 by hypothesis and n≥1\mathrm{n}\geq 1. Hence e=t+1\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}+1 and σ⁡(S)=Θ⁡(S)=0\sigma(S)=\Theta(S)=0, and the latter gives c=(t+1)​n\mathrm{c}=(\mathrm{t}+1)\mathrm{n} by (16).

(ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (iii). By Theorem 6.3, SS is symmetric or S=Tm,kS=T_{\mathrm{m},k} with m≥3\mathrm{m}\geq 3. If SS is symmetric then t=1\mathrm{t}=1 by Lemma 2.1(iii), so e=t+1=2\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}+1=2.

(iii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i). If e=2\mathrm{e}=2 then SS is symmetric by Lemma 2.1(vii), so g=c/2\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{c}/2 and n=c−g=c/2\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{c}/2, whence W⁡(S)=2⋅(c/2)−c=0\mathrm{W}(S)=2\cdot(\mathrm{c}/2)-\mathrm{c}=0. If S=Tm,kS=T_{\mathrm{m},k} then W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 by Lemma 2.3. ∎

Only the implication (i) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii) uses the hypothesis e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1; the equivalence (ii) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (iii) and the implication (iii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i) hold for every numerical semigroup S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N}. Indeed (iii) already forces e=t+1\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}+1: if e=2\mathrm{e}=2 then SS is symmetric and t=1\mathrm{t}=1 by Lemma 2.1(iii) and (vii), while S=Tm,kS=T_{\mathrm{m},k} has e=m=t+1\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{t}+1 by Lemma 2.3. What Theorem 6.4 leaves open is therefore precisely whether W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 forces e⁡(S)=t⁡(S)+1\mathrm{e}(S)=\mathrm{t}(S)+1.

By Lemma 2.3, Theorem 6.4 answers [18, Question 8] for every numerical semigroup with e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1. Since Corollary 4.6 places the locus {Θ=0}\{\Theta=0\} inside the FGH range, the theorem also settles the equality case for every SS with Θ⁡(S)=0\Theta(S)=0.

Remark 6.5.

The hypothesis e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1 in Theorem 6.4 cannot be removed by the present method. By (7), a numerical semigroup with W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 and e≤t\mathrm{e}\leq\mathrm{t} would satisfy σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)=(t+1−e)​n≥n\sigma(S)+\Theta(S)=(\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e})\mathrm{n}\geq\mathrm{n}, and excluding this would require control of g\mathrm{g} in the range e≤t\mathrm{e}\leq\mathrm{t}, where Conjecture 1.1 is itself open.

7. Semigroups with c≤2​m\mathrm{c}\leq 2\mathrm{m}: a correction

This section rests only on Lemma 2.3 and is independent of Sections 4–6. Theorem 6.4 settled the equality case W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 throughout the FGH range; a second unbounded range, c≤2​m\mathrm{c}\leq 2\mathrm{m}, is not contained in the first, since Example 4.7 has c=2​m\mathrm{c}=2\mathrm{m} and e<t\mathrm{e}<\mathrm{t}. The outcome corrects [16, Proposition 26]. The correction concerns only the list of equality cases: [16, Theorem 24] and every other result of [16] are unaffected. The combinatorial input is the following notion.

Definition 7.1.

A finite set B={b1,…,ba}⊆ℕB=\{b_{1},\dots,b_{a}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N} with 0∈B0\in B is a perfect additive basis of order 22 if the sums bi+bjb_{i}+b_{j} with i≤ji\leq j constitute the interval [0,(a+12)−1]∩ℤ\bigl[0,\binom{a+1}{2}-1\bigr]\cap\mathbb{Z}. Since that interval has (a+12)\binom{a+1}{2} elements and there are exactly (a+12)\binom{a+1}{2} such sums, the sums are then pairwise distinct.

Lemma 7.2.

The only perfect additive bases of order 22 are B={0}B=\{0\} and B={0,1}B=\{0,1\}; in particular such a BB has at most two elements.

Proof.

For a=1a=1 the unique candidate is B={0}B=\{0\}, with sum set {0}\{0\}; for a=2a=2, B={0,b}B=\{0,b\} has sums 0,b,2​b0,b,2b, and these form {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\} exactly when b=1b=1.

Suppose a≥3a\geq 3 and put N=(a+12)=a⁡(a+1)/2≥6N=\binom{a+1}{2}=a(a+1)/2\geq 6, so that the sum set is [0,N−1][0,N-1]. The integer 11 must be a sum bi+bjb_{i}+b_{j}; as all elements of BB are nonnegative and two positive elements sum to at least 22, necessarily 1=0+11=0+1 and so 1∈B1\in B. Then 2=1+12=1+1 is a representation of 22; if also 2∈B2\in B then 2=0+22=0+2 would be a second one, contradicting distinctness, so 2∉B2\notin B. Since N−1≥5N-1\geq 5, the integer 33 lies in the sum set; the only possible representations are 0+30+3 and 1+21+2, and the latter is excluded, so 3∈B3\in B. Then 4=1+34=1+3; if 4∈B4\in B then 4=0+44=0+4 would be a second representation, so 4∉B4\notin B. Since N−1≥5N-1\geq 5, the integer 55 lies in the sum set, and its possible representations 0+50+5, 1+41+4, 2+32+3 leave only 5∈B5\in B.

We have shown {0,1,3,5}⊆B\{0,1,3,5\}\subseteq B. If a=3a=3 this contradicts |B|=3|B|=3. If a≥4a\geq 4 then N−1≥9≥6N-1\geq 9\geq 6, so 66 lies in the sum set; but 6=3+3=1+56=3+3=1+5 are two distinct representations, a contradiction. Hence a≤2a\leq 2. ∎

This yields the corrected classification.

Theorem 7.3.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup with c⁡(S)≤2​m​(S)\mathrm{c}(S)\leq 2\mathrm{m}(S). Then W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 if and only if

S=Tm,1=⟨m,m+1,…,2​m−1⟩orS=Tm,2=⟨m,2​m+1,…,3​m−1⟩(m≥2),S=T_{\mathrm{m},1}=\langle\mathrm{m},\mathrm{m}+1,\dots,2\mathrm{m}-1\rangle\quad\text{or}\quad S=T_{\mathrm{m},2}=\langle\mathrm{m},2\mathrm{m}+1,\dots,3\mathrm{m}-1\rangle\qquad(\mathrm{m}\geq 2),

or S=⟨3,4⟩S=\langle 3,4\rangle.

Remark 7.4.

The family Tm,2T_{\mathrm{m},2} is absent from [16, Proposition 26] for the following reason. In the notation of that proof, SS is written as ⟨m,k1​m+1,…,km−2​m+m−2,2​m+m−1⟩\langle\mathrm{m},k_{1}\mathrm{m}+1,\dots,k_{\mathrm{m}-2}\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}-2,2\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{m}-1\rangle and RR denotes the number of indices ii with ki=1k_{i}=1; the argument concludes by observing that a certain expression equals R⁡[(R+1)​(R+2)/2−m]R\bigl[(R+1)(R+2)/2-\mathrm{m}\bigr] and is nonnegative “if and only if (R+1)​(R+2)≥2​m(R+1)(R+2)\geq 2\mathrm{m}”. That equivalence fails at R=0R=0, where the expression vanishes identically for every m\mathrm{m}. The case R=0R=0 is exactly Ap⁡(S,m)={0,2​m+1,2​m+2,…,3​m−1}\Ap(S,\mathrm{m})=\{0,2\mathrm{m}+1,2\mathrm{m}+2,\dots,3\mathrm{m}-1\}, that is, S=Tm,2S=T_{\mathrm{m},2}. The family occurs explicitly in [16] as an example showing that F<2​m\mathrm{F}<2\mathrm{m} does not imply 2​g<3​m2\mathrm{g}<3\mathrm{m}.

Remark 7.5.

Every semigroup listed in Theorem 7.3 satisfies e=t+1\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}+1, by Lemma 2.3 for Tm,1T_{\mathrm{m},1} and Tm,2T_{\mathrm{m},2} and directly for ⟨3,4⟩\langle 3,4\rangle. Hence W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 implies e⁡(S)=t⁡(S)+1\mathrm{e}(S)=\mathrm{t}(S)+1 on the whole range c≤2​m\mathrm{c}\leq 2\mathrm{m}.

Theorems 6.4 and 7.3 settle the equality case on two unbounded ranges, neither containing the other, and on each of them W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 forces e=t+1\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}+1. We conjecture that no hypothesis is needed.

Conjecture 7.6.

Let S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} be a numerical semigroup with W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0. Then e⁡(S)=t⁡(S)+1\mathrm{e}(S)=\mathrm{t}(S)+1; consequently e⁡(S)=2\mathrm{e}(S)=2, or S=Tm,kS=T_{\mathrm{m},k} for some m≥3\mathrm{m}\geq 3 and k≥1k\geq 1.

The second assertion is [18, Question 8]; the first is stronger, and by Remark 6.5 any proof of it outside the FGH range must control g\mathrm{g} in the regime e≤t\mathrm{e}\leq\mathrm{t}.

8. Computational verification

No proof in this paper depends on a computation: every theorem, proposition and corollary above is established by an argument that is self-contained modulo the standard facts collected in Lemma 2.1, and the examples are verified by hand in the text. The computations reported here serve as an independent check of those results and as the evidence for Conjectures 4.9, 5.2 and 7.6.

We enumerated numerical semigroups by genus using the standard tree in which the children of SS are the semigroups S∖{x}S\setminus\{x\} with xx a primitive element of SS satisfying x>F⁡(S)x>\mathrm{F}(S); the root ℕ\mathbb{N} is handled separately, its unique child being ℕ∖{1}\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}. The enumeration was validated against the counting sequence NgN_{\mathrm{g}} of numerical semigroups of genus g\mathrm{g},

1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 23, 39, 67, 118, 204, 343, 592, 1001, 1693, 2857,…,1,\,1,\,2,\,4,\,7,\,12,\,23,\,39,\,67,\,118,\,204,\,343,\,592,\,1001,\,1693,\,2857,\dots,

which our program reproduces exactly up to g=31\mathrm{g}=31, where N31=9,266,788N_{31}=9{,}266{,}788 (see [2, 15]).

For each semigroup we computed m,F,c,g,n,e,t\mathrm{m},\mathrm{F},\mathrm{c},\mathrm{g},\mathrm{n},\mathrm{e},\mathrm{t}, the set PF⁡(S)\PF(S), the Apéry sets Ap⁡(S,s)\Ap(S,s) and the order relations of Qs​(S)Q_{s}(S), the functions λS\lambda_{S} and νS\nu_{S}, the invariants Λ,σ,Θ\Lambda,\sigma,\Theta of Definition 3.1, the quantity Ξ\Xi of (11), and the Wilf number. The following assertions, listed in the order in which the paper states them, were tested and held without exception over all 23,663,12523{,}663{,}125 numerical semigroups S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} of genus at most 3131:

  1. (V1)

    W⁡(S)≥0\mathrm{W}(S)\geq 0 (Conjecture 1.1, reconfirming [7] in this range);

    the identity W⁡(S)=(e−t−1)​n+σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)\mathrm{W}(S)=(\mathrm{e}-\mathrm{t}-1)\mathrm{n}+\sigma(S)+\Theta(S) of Proposition 3.2;

    the bound (10) holds for every s∈L⁡(S)∖{0}s\in\mathrm{L}(S)\setminus\{0\}; and the identifications Min⁡Qs​(S)\Min Q_{s}(S) and Max⁡Qs​(S)\Max Q_{s}(S) of Lemma 4.1 hold, again for every such ss, as equalities of sets and not merely of cardinalities. The latter check is cubic in F\mathrm{F} and was run over the 258,581258{,}581 numerical semigroups of genus at most 2222;

  4. (V4)

    t≤∑p∈P∖{m}νS​(p−m)≤e−1+Ξ⁡(S)≤e−1+Θ⁡(S)\mathrm{t}\leq\sum_{p\in P\setminus\{\mathrm{m}\}}\nu_{S}(p-\mathrm{m})\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\Xi(S)\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\Theta(S) (Theorem 4.4);

    g+σ⁡(S)≤e−1+t⁡(n−1)\mathrm{g}+\sigma(S)\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\mathrm{t}(\mathrm{n}-1) (Corollary 4.8);

    t≤e−1+σ⁡(S)\mathrm{t}\leq\mathrm{e}-1+\sigma(S) (Conjecture 4.9);

  7. (V7)

    Θ⁡(S)≥∑i=1dλS​(fi)\Theta(S)\geq\sum_{i=1}^{d}\lambda_{S}(f_{i}) whenever t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e} (Conjecture 5.2);

    m≥K+1\mathrm{m}\geq K+1, [ℓ+1,F]⊆PF⁡(S)[\ell+1,\mathrm{F}]\subseteq\PF(S), and σ⁡(S)=0\sigma(S)=0 if and only if PF⁡(S)=[ℓ+1,F]\PF(S)=[\ell+1,\mathrm{F}], where ℓ=max⁡L\ell=\max\mathrm{L} and K=F−ℓK=\mathrm{F}-\ell (Lemma 6.1);

  11. (V11)

    W⁡(S)=0\mathrm{W}(S)=0 if and only if e=2\mathrm{e}=2 or S=Tm,kS=T_{\mathrm{m},k} for some m≥3\mathrm{m}\geq 3 and k≥1k\geq 1, with no hypothesis relating e\mathrm{e} and t\mathrm{t}, and in that case e=t+1\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}+1 (Conjecture 7.6).

Item (V11) goes beyond what is proved here: Theorem 6.4 establishes Conjecture 7.6 under the hypothesis e≥t+1\mathrm{e}\geq\mathrm{t}+1 and Theorem 7.3 for c≤2​m\mathrm{c}\leq 2\mathrm{m}, and since the enumeration is exhaustive, the computation shows that no counterexample with e≤t\mathrm{e}\leq\mathrm{t} occurs in the range g≤31\mathrm{g}\leq 31. Every numerical semigroup of genus at most 3131 with e≤t\mathrm{e}\leq\mathrm{t} satisfies W⁡(S)≥2\mathrm{W}(S)\geq 2; the value 22 is attained at genus 1010, for instance by ⟨7,8,10,19⟩\langle 7,8,10,19\rangle and ⟨7,9,10,15⟩\langle 7,9,10,15\rangle, both of which have e=t=4\mathrm{e}=\mathrm{t}=4, n=4\mathrm{n}=4 and c=14\mathrm{c}=14.

Items (V6) and (V7) were tested, without exception, over all 171,202,689171{,}202{,}689 numerical semigroups S≠ℕS\neq\mathbb{N} of genus at most 3535, among which 9,559,6599{,}559{,}659 satisfy t≥e\mathrm{t}\geq\mathrm{e}. Conjecture 4.9 is sharp in that range, its slack being 00; Conjecture 5.2 is not, its slack being at least 22 throughout. The minimal slack 22 is attained, for instance, by the semigroup S=⟨9,10,12,13⟩S=\langle 9,10,12,13\rangle of Example 4.7, where d=2d=2, PF⁡(S)={11,14,15,16,17}\PF(S)=\{11,14,15,16,17\}, Θ⁡(S)=10\Theta(S)=10 and λS​(11)+λS​(14)=3+5=8\lambda_{S}(11)+\lambda_{S}(14)=3+5=8.

The enumeration also shows that, among the 23,663,12523{,}663{,}125 semigroups of genus at most 3131, exactly 23,61223{,}612 satisfy Θ⁡(S)=0\Theta(S)=0, and Ξ⁡(S)<Θ⁡(S)\Xi(S)<\Theta(S) holds for all but 24,09424{,}094. The locus Θ=0\Theta=0 is thus sparse, in accordance with Theorem 4.4: vanishing Θ\Theta forces the Apéry poset to have at least as many minimal as maximal elements.

9. Concluding remarks

Outside the FGH range the identity (7) makes Conjecture 1.1 equivalent to

σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)≥(t⁡(S)+1−e⁡(S))​n​(S),\sigma(S)+\Theta(S)\;\geq\;\bigl(\mathrm{t}(S)+1-\mathrm{e}(S)\bigr)\,\mathrm{n}(S),

and Theorem 4.4 supplies Θ⁡(S)≥t+1−e\Theta(S)\geq\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e}. Conjecture 4.9 would supply the same for σ⁡(S)\sigma(S), and the two together give σ⁡(S)+Θ⁡(S)≥2​(t+1−e)\sigma(S)+\Theta(S)\geq 2(\mathrm{t}+1-\mathrm{e}): the displayed inequality with n\mathrm{n} replaced by 22. The remaining discrepancy is a factor of n/2\mathrm{n}/2, and it is what the bounds established here leave open.

The three conjectures that remain open concern the regime e≤t\mathrm{e}\leq\mathrm{t}, in which the type has so far contributed nothing. Conjecture 7.6 asserts that the equality case is confined to the FGH range. Conjecture 5.2 is of a different order: by Proposition 5.3 it implies Conjecture 1.1 outright, and by Remark 5.4 it is no easier.
